questions.stem: Which intellectual property right protects a new invention or process?
questions.why: Patents protect inventions for a fixed period. Copyright protects creative work, and trademarks protect names and logos.
whyNot: Copyright protects original written, musical, artistic and software work.
A trademark protects a name, logo or slogan.
A licence is permission to trade or to use someone else's property.

questions.stem: Which right protects a business's name, logo or slogan?
questions.why: Trademarks stop a competitor trading under your name, which is what makes brand investment worth making.
whyNot: Patents protect inventions.
Copyright protects creative works.
A quality standard is a measurable level of quality, not a legal right.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of competition policy?
options: Laws preventing businesses from abusing market power, such as price fixing or predatory pricing
Laws requiring goods to be fit for purpose
questions.why: Competition policy protects the market from abuse of dominance. It helps small businesses far more than it hinders them.
whyNot: That is consumer protection.
That is employee protection.
That is environmental protection.

questions.stem: Why is intellectual property legislation mostly a benefit to a business?
options: It makes a USP defensible, so innovation is worth funding
It reduces the cost of raw materials
It removes the need to advertise
questions.why: Without a patent a competitor copies the invention immediately, and without a trademark anyone can trade under your name. Protection is what makes investment in innovation rational.
whyNot: No connection to input costs.
A protected brand still has to be communicated.
Patents last a fixed period, not forever.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit to a business of employee protection legislation?
options: Better motivated staff and lower labour turnover
questions.why: Better treated staff are more motivated and stay longer, which reduces the recruitment and training cycle. It connects directly to staff as an asset in WBS11 topic 1.3.4.1.
whyNot: It typically raises the wage bill through minimum wage and entitlements.
It restricts dismissal, requiring fair procedure.
Contracts are a legal requirement.

questions.stem: Why is environmental legislation closer to protecting revenue than imposing a burden in a tourism-dependent economy?
options: A damaged reef or polluted lagoon destroys the product the industry sells
Environmental laws are not enforced in tourism
questions.why: Where the environment IS the product, protecting it protects long-term revenue. No marketing recovers a destroyed reef, which makes this a strong example for the balanced argument about legislation.
whyNot: Waste, sewage and construction rules are enforced precisely because the stakes are high.
Resorts and guesthouses generate substantial waste and sewage.
Compliance costs real money; the point is what it protects.

questions.stem: Why does the burden of legislation fall hardest on small businesses?
options: They have no legal or HR department, so compliance takes the owner's own time
The law applies only to small businesses
Large businesses are exempt from most laws
questions.why: Compliance is largely a fixed cost, so it is proportionately heavier for a small firm, and it consumes the owner's time, which is their scarcest resource.
whyNot: It applies to businesses of all sizes.
Fines are usually scaled to size or turnover.
Large businesses face more regulation, not less.

questions.stem: What is the strongest argument that compliance is worth the cost?
options: Fines, compensation and reputational damage generally exceed the cost of doing it properly
Legislation has no cost at all
questions.why: Comparing the cost of compliance with the cost of breach is the balanced argument, and it is what turns a list of costs into an evaluation.
whyNot: Compliance has real costs.
Detection is common, particularly in regulated sectors.
It clearly does have costs; the point is the comparison.
